analysis.title: Reminiscence of things past
key_insights: The S&P 500 keeps making new highs but breadth is deteriorating: more than 75% of index constituents are at least 10% below their 52-week highs and 37% are down more than 20%.
Concentration is at a historic extreme: the five largest stocks carry as much market capitalization as the bottom 434 combined.
The Nasdaq 100 keeps pushing higher while the equal-weighted Value Line index has been rolling over since August, so the gap between winners and the rest is widening.
The cumulative advance-decline line has fallen back toward its spring lows even as the S&P 500 holds near record highs, meaning fewer stocks are doing the heavy lifting.
The gap between the S&P 500 and its ex-AI counterpart has widened sharply, so the market is increasingly a bet on one theme rather than a broad bull market.

Dot-com analog: Cisco peaked in March 2000 while Juniper Networks kept rallying until October as speculative capital rotated into next-generation winners. Today Nvidia holds up while second-tier AI names have drawn down, with CoreWeave about 50% below its 2025 high and SpaceX about 25% below its post-IPO peak.
The AI Big 10 account for 42% of the market, in line with the Nifty Fifty, Japan and dot-com bubble peaks. Only the railroad mania went materially further.
The Shiller PE is 41.8x, approaching its November 1999 peak of 44.2x. Valuations are poor timing tools, and nobody knows which month of 1999 the market is in.
risk_factors: Narrow leadership: the index depends on a handful of AI names while most stocks are in correction territory.
Second-tier AI names (CoreWeave, SpaceX) have already suffered large drawdowns, a pattern similar to late-cycle 2000.
Valuations near dot-com levels (Shiller PE 41.8x vs 44.2x in November 1999), with the timing of any reversal unknowable.
